Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Vignette:
Arthur Hayes had spent forty years as a combat pilot, learning to read atmospheric shear and trust the weight of his harness. He did not trust the hands that belonged to David, his husband of seven years. The abuse began quietly, a heavy grip on his bicep that tightened during arguments, before escalating to shoves against the kitchen door and a palm pressed hard against his sternum. David’s temper always arrived with the sharp, yeasty scent of whiskey, and Arthur learned to read the set of his jaw, the silver catching the morning light, the exact way his boots would scrape the linoleum before a strike. Arthur survived by staying perfectly still, but the violence left a permanent imprint. He could not unlearn the shape of a hand on his shoulder, the sight of a man who moved with that same aggressive roll of the shoulders, or the sudden tang of aged spirits on a breath. At seventy-four, Arthur still reported to the municipal airfield as a senior flight safety consultant. The morning briefing room became a map he memorized, noting every chair, every window, every potential exit. He sat with his back to the drywall, his eyes tracking the door handle during staff updates. When a colleague approached to hand him a flight deck report, Arthur’s chest tightened, his forearms locked, and a sudden wave of heat rushed to his face. He accepted the folder without looking up, his voice flat, his jaw unyielding. He considered anger a structural flaw. He swallowed the heat, let his hands rest calmly on his thighs, and returned to the checklist. His professional routine shifted accordingly. He declined a lead mentorship position. The required weekly strategy sessions demanded sitting shoulder-to-shoulder with junior officers, a proximity he found impossible to sustain alongside his need to remain alert and unobstructed. The habits formed over months, then years. Arthur altered his evening walks to avoid the bar on Fourth Street, where he once saw David across the street and felt his breath catch, his knees going rigid until the man turned the corner. He stepped back when a visitor at the airfield smelled of bourbon on his coffee break, his stomach dropping as if he were still pinned against that kitchen wall. He kept his personal conversations strictly functional, declining invitations to neighborhood gatherings and leaving coffee dates before the conversation turned to memories or feelings. He told himself it was efficiency, but the reality was simpler: closeness required opening a door he had spent decades keeping bolted. He slept poorly, lying awake with his muscles coiled, certain that dropping his watchfulness even for a few hours would leave him exposed. When he finally drifted off, his body would jerk awake, heart pounding, breath coming short, entirely separate from the quiet of his own bedroom. The tipping point arrived on a Thursday in October. During a routine aircraft inspection, a junior pilot reached over to point at a control panel, his sleeve brushing Arthur’s wrist. The contact was brief, incidental, but Arthur’s pulse hammered against his ribs, his throat closed, and the familiar metallic taste of adrenaline flooded his mouth. He walked out of the hangar, sat in his truck with the engine off, and stared at the flight line until the sky turned gray. He knew he could not navigate the hangar and his own nervous system alone. He called the veterans’ health clinic that evening, requesting an intake appointment. He told the scheduling clerk he wanted to learn how to rest without bracing for impact, but in the quiet of his kitchen afterward, he recognized what he actually needed: a place where he could finally lower his shoulders, where the past would stop reaching for him in the dark, and where he might, just perhaps, allow himself to feel the anger he had spent so long holding back.
